Preface
This dictionary is a concise reference to medical terms, diseases, investigations, treatments, anatomy,
physiology, and related clinical concepts. It is intended to help students, healthcare professionals, educators,
and general readers understand unfamiliar medical language.
The entries are arranged alphabetically from A to Z, with each letter presented in its own chapter. This
arrangement allows a reader to locate a known term quickly while maintaining a consistent structure
throughout the book. Related terms, recognized common names, and alternative names are included when
they improve clarity or aid searching.
Definitions are written in simple, formal language and are intended to be clear, accurate, and useful for
reference. Medical terminology changes as scientific knowledge and clinical guidance develop; therefore,
important information should be checked against current textbooks, primary research, professional guidance,
and local clinical protocols.
This book is an educational reference, not a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis, or
treatment. Readers should seek advice from a qualified healthcare professional when making decisions
about health.
Chaman Singh Verma


Medical Disclaimer
Educational and Reference Purpose Only: This publication, The Modern Medical Pocket Dictionary,
is prepared and compiled strictly for educational, academic, historical, and reference purposes. It is intended
for medical students, healthcare professionals, educators, and researchers.
No Medical Advice: The information contained herein does not constitute professional medical advice,
clinical diagnosis, treatment protocols, or formal therapeutic recommendations. It should not be used as a
substitute for the professional judgment of qualified physicians, surgeons, or certified healthcare providers.
Clinical Practice Guidelines: Healthcare practitioners must always consult primary evidence-based
medical literature, institutional protocols, manufacturer prescribing information, and national clinical
guidelines (such as WHO, CDC, NICE, or national medical councils) when making diagnostic or therapeutic
decisions for individual patients.
Limitation of Liability: Neither the author nor the publishers accept any legal responsibility or liability
for any errors, omissions, or clinical outcomes resulting from the use or application of any information
presented in this work.

Azotemia
A build-up of nitrogen-containing waste products in
the blood, usually because the kidneys are filtering
less effectively. It may occur with dehydration,
reduced kidney blood flow, or kidney disease.

superior vena cava. It provides an alternate route
for blood when major veins are blocked.

Butyric Acid
Butyric acid is a short-chain fatty acid produced
by gut bacteria during fiber fermentation and used
by colon cells as an energy source; concentrated
exposure irritates tissue.

Bx
A common medical abbreviation for biopsy, the re-
moval of cells or tissue for microscopic or laboratory
examination.

By-Pass
A route made around a blocked or narrowed passage.
In medicine, a bypass may redirect blood, food,
bile, urine, or another fluid through a natural or
surgically created pathway.

Bypass
Creation of an alternative route around a blocked or
narrowed passage. A bypass can restore blood flow
or redirect body contents, using a natural pathway,
tube, vein, or artificial graft depending on the organ
involved.

Bypass Graft
A vein or artificial tube surgically connected to
route blood around a blocked or weakened artery.
Grafts are used in coronary, leg, and aortic opera-
tions; blood flow, infection, clotting, and long-term
narrowing affect their durability.

Bypass Surgery
An operation that creates a new route around a
blocked or diseased passage. Examples include coro-
nary and leg-artery bypasses and gastric bypass;
possible complications include bleeding, infection,
clotting, and narrowing of the connection.

Dystrophy
Abnormal development, maintenance, or degenera-
tion of a tissue or organ, often caused by an inherited
or metabolic condition. Effects depend on the tis-
sue and may include muscle weakness, poor vision,
fragile structures, or loss of function.

Dysuria
Pain, burning, or discomfort during urination. Com-

vaginal or penile inflammation, stones, irritation,
and sexually transmitted infections; fever, flank
pain, pregnancy, or blood in urine needs medical
assessment.

Déjà Vu
A feeling that a current situation has happened be-
fore, even though it is probably new. Occasional
episodes are common; frequent episodes with im-
paired awareness or unusual movements may occur
with seizures.

706
Eyelid Twitch
Alternate name; see Eye Twitching.

Eyelids
Movable folds of skin, muscle, and glands that pro-
tect the eyes, spread tears, and help control light.
Their position and movement are important for
keeping the eye surface moist and safe.

Eyesight
Alternate name; see Vision.

Eyestrain
Tired, dry, sore, or uncomfortable eyes, sometimes
with blurred vision or headache, after prolonged vi-
sual effort. Screen use, glare, poor lighting, dry eye,
or an uncorrected focusing problem may contribute;
rest often helps.

Ezetimibe
An oral medicine that reduces absorption of choles-
terol from the intestine. It lowers blood cholesterol
alone or with another medicine and may cause diar-
rhea, abdominal discomfort, or rarely liver or muscle
problems.

Idiopathic Edema
Persistent swelling, usually of the legs, occurring
without an identified heart, kidney, liver, venous,
lymphatic, or medication-related cause. The diag-
nosis is one of exclusion and requires evaluation for
more common causes before treatment.

Optical Aids
Eyeglasses correct focusing errors, sunglasses re-
duce glare and ultraviolet exposure, and magnifiers
enlarge nearby targets. Correct prescription, fit,
lens protection, and the underlying eye condition
determine the appropriate aid.
Alternate Names:
Corrective Eyewear; Eyeglasses; Eyeglasses and
Sunglasses; Eyeglasses, Sunglasses, and Magnifiers;
Magnifiers; Sunglasses; Visual Aids

Gyrate Atrophy
An inherited retinal disorder causing gradually wors-
ening peripheral and night vision loss. It results
from abnormal ornithine metabolism and may be
managed with dietary treatment, supplements, and
regular eye monitoring.

Gyrus
A raised fold on the surface of the brain, sepa-
rated from neighboring folds by grooves called sulci.
These folds increase the cerebral cortex’s surface
area within the skull and contain areas responsible
for different functions.

Physical Abuse
Deliberate use of physical force that causes or risks
injury, pain, disability, or death. In clinical care,
suspected abuse requires attention to immediate
safety, documentation, and reporting duties under
local law.

Quit Smoking
Alternate name; see Smoking Cessation.

Quorum Sensing
A density-dependent bacterial intercellular commu-
nication mechanism mediated by the release and
detection of small diffusible autoinducer signaling
molecules, coordinating group behaviors such as
biofilm formation, bioluminescence, and virulence
factor expression once a threshold bacterial popula-
tion density is achieved.

Quotidian Fever
A fever pattern in which fever rises or attacks occur
about every 24 hours. It can occur with malaria
and other infections, but the timing of fever alone
does not identify the cause.

Quotidian Malaria
A recurring pattern of malarial paroxysms charac-
terized by daily febrile spikes occurring at 24-hour
intervals, classic for infection caused by Plasmod-
ium knowlesi or resulting from overlapping broods
of Plasmodium vivax or Plasmodium falciparum.
Alternate Names:
24-Hour Malarial Paroxysm; Daily Malarial Fever

Q Wave
A downward movement that may begin the electrical
pattern of a heartbeat on an electrocardiogram. It
can be normal in some recording positions or suggest
previous heart-muscle injury, depending on its size
and location.

Q Waves
Early downward waves on an electrocardiogram.
Some patterns may suggest a previous heart attack
or another heart problem, but Q waves must be
interpreted with the other ECG findings and the
person’s history.
Alternate Names:
Pathologic Q Wave; Myocardial Infarction Q Wave

Synergistic Necrotizing Fasciitis
A rapidly progressive necrotizing soft-tissue infec-
tion caused by mixed aerobic and anaerobic organ-
isms acting together. Severe pain, swelling, skin
discoloration, fever, toxicity, or rapid progression
requires immediate surgery, antibiotics, and critical
care.

Systemic Aleukemic Reticuloendotheliosis
A historical name for a leukemic reticuloendothe-
lial disorder, most often referring to the aleukemic
form of hairy-cell leukemia. It may cause low blood
counts, an enlarged spleen, infections, fatigue, or
bleeding and is diagnosed by blood, marrow, and
immunophenotypic studies.

U Wave                                                   Ulcerative Colitis (UC)
A small wave that may appear after the T wave            Alternate name; see Ulcerative Colitis.
on an electrocardiogram. A prominent U wave can
occur with low potassium, a slow heart rate, or
some medicines and must be interpreted with the

Underactive Thyroid
Alternate name; see Hypothyroidism.

Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)
Alternate name; see Urinary Tract Infection.

Ureteral Stones
Stones lodged in a ureter, the tube carrying urine
from a kidney to the bladder. They may cause
severe wave-like flank or groin pain, blood in the
urine, nausea, blockage, or infection and sometimes
need urgent treatment.

Uterine Polyp
A growth arising from the inner lining of the uterus.
Many are benign, but they can cause irregular or
heavy bleeding, bleeding after menopause, or infertil-
ity and may require imaging, sampling, or removal.

Universal Precautions
Infection-control practices that treat blood and cer-
tain body fluids as potentially infectious, regardless
of a person’s diagnosed condition. They include
hand hygiene, appropriate gloves and protective
barriers, safe sharps handling, and measures to pre-
vent exposure to bloodborne pathogens.

Vulvovaginal Candidiasis
A yeast infection of the vulva and vagina, usually
caused by Candida. It commonly causes intense itch-
ing, burning, soreness, redness, and thick discharge;
recurrent, severe, unusual, or treatment-resistant
symptoms need testing to confirm the cause.

Vulvovaginitis
Simultaneous inflammation or infection of the vulva
and vagina, commonly presenting with pruritus,
burning, dysuria, dyspareunia, and abnormal vagi-
nal discharge, resulting from infectious etiologies
(such as Candida albicans, Bacterial vaginosis, Tri-
chomonas vaginalis) or non-infectious causes (at-
rophic vaginitis, contact irritants).
Alternate Names:
Vaginitis and Vulvitis; Vulvovaginal Inflammation

Vocal Cord Disorders
Disorders affecting the vocal folds or their nerves, in-
cluding nodules, polyps, cysts, inflammation, paral-
ysis, spasmodic dysphonia, and paradoxical vocal-
fold movement. They may cause hoarseness, voice
loss, throat discomfort, noisy breathing, or difficulty
breathing and swallowing.

Vocal Cord Dysfunction
Inappropriate closing or narrowing of the vocal folds,
especially during inhalation, causing sudden throat
tightness, noisy breathing, cough, or shortness of
breath that can resemble asthma. It is also called in-
ducible laryngeal obstruction and needs assessment
when breathing is difficult.

Wisdom Tooth Removal
Dental extraction of one or more third molars, com-
monly performed when they are impacted, repeat-
edly infected, decayed, or damaging adjacent teeth.
Risks include pain, infection, bleeding, dry socket,

Alternate spelling of Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome, a
rare disorder caused by deletion of part of chro-
mosome 4 and associated with growth restriction,
seizures, developmental disability, and distinctive
facial features.

Wolf Syndrome
Alternate name for Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome, a
chromosome 4 deletion disorder affecting growth,
development, and multiple organ systems.

WPW Syndrome
Abbreviation for Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome,
a pre-excitation disorder in which an extra electri-
cal pathway can cause episodes of supraventricular
tachycardia. Palpitations, fainting, chest pain, or
severe breathlessness require prompt assessment.

Wells Syndrome
Eosinophilic cellulitis, an uncommon inflammatory
skin disorder causing itchy or burning red plaques,
swelling, blisters, or a cellulitis-like eruption with-
out typical bacterial infection. Blood eosinophilia
and a skin biopsy may support the diagnosis, and
recurrences are possible.

Urine Drug Screen
A preliminary urine test that looks for selected
medicines or recreational drugs and their breakdown
products. Results can be falsely positive or negative
and may need confirmation with a more specific
laboratory test.

A.C. A prescription abbreviation meaning “before meals,” from the Latin ante cibum.
ALA An abbreviation for alpha-linolenic acid, an essential omega-3 fatty acid, or aminolevulinic acid, a heme-pathway
   compound used topically in some photodynamic treatments; context determines the meaning.
AP An abbreviation commonly meaning anteroposterior, or directed from front to back; in some contexts it may
   have another medical expansion.
ATM An abbreviation that may mean the temporomandibular joint or ataxia-telangiectasia mutated, a protein
   kinase involved in DNA-damage repair; context determines the meaning.


2156
BF Physician’s shorthand for Black female; demographic abbreviations should be used cautiously and replaced with
   precise, patient-preferred language when possible.
BPD An abbreviation commonly meaning bronchopulmonary dysplasia, chronic lung disease after premature birth;
   it can also mean borderline personality disorder in psychiatric contexts.
CA A medical abbreviation that may mean cancer, carcinoma, or calcium; the intended meaning depends on the
   surrounding clinical context.
CKD Abbreviation for Chronic Kidney Disease: a progressive loss of kidney function over months to years, defined
   by a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) less than 60 mL/min/1.73m2 or markers of kidney damage (albuminuria,
   haematuria, structural abnormalities) persisting for at least 3 months.
CLA An abbreviation that commonly means conjugated linoleic acid, a group of fatty-acid isomers; in other medical
   contexts it may have a different expansion.
CTG Abbreviation for cardiotocography; continuous electronic monitoring of fetal heart rate and uterine contractions
   during labour.
CVA An abbreviation for cerebrovascular accident, meaning a stroke caused by interruption of blood flow to the
   brain or bleeding within the brain. It may cause sudden neurologic deficits.
CVS An abbreviation that may mean cardiovascular system or chorionic-villus sampling, a prenatal diagnostic
   procedure; context determines the meaning.
DDAVP The abbreviation for desmopressin, a synthetic vasopressin-like medicine used for some bleeding disorders,
   central diabetes insipidus, and nighttime urination.
DES An abbreviation that may mean diethylstilbestrol, a synthetic estrogen, or drug-eluting stent; diethylstilbestrol
   exposure during pregnancy is associated with later reproductive and cancer risks.
DHHS The abbreviation for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
DNR An abbreviation for do-not-resuscitate, indicating that cardiopulmonary resuscitation should not be attempted
  if breathing or heartbeat stops.
DNS An abbreviation that may mean deviated nasal septum or dextrose in normal saline; the intended expansion
   depends on the clinical context.
DPT An older abbreviation for the combined diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus vaccine; current formulations include
   DTaP and Tdap.
DT An abbreviation that may mean delirium tremens or diphtheria–tetanus vaccine; the intended meaning depends
   on context.
DTC An abbreviation that may mean differentiated thyroid carcinoma or direct-to-consumer, such as direct-to-
   consumer genetic testing; the intended meaning depends on context.
DTP An older abbreviation for diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis vaccine; current childhood formulations are
   generally called DTaP.
DV An abbreviation that may mean domestic violence, ductus venosus, or another context-specific term; the full
   expression should be specified.
DYS An abbreviation or word root related to dysplasia, dystonia, dyslexia, or another condition beginning with
   dys-; the intended meaning depends on context.
EC An abbreviation that may mean enteric-coated, emergency contraception, or endothelial cell; the intended
   meaning depends on context.
EFT An abbreviation whose medical meaning depends on context, such as endocrine-function testing or emotional
   freedom technique; the intended expansion should be specified.
ENT Abbreviation for ear, nose, and throat; it commonly refers to the otolaryngology specialty or an otolaryngologist.


                                                                                                                2157
EOS Commonly an abbreviation for eosinophils or an eosinophil count in laboratory reports; the intended meaning
   should be confirmed from the report’s context.
EPA Abbreviation for eicosapentaenoic acid, an omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid found in oily fish and fish-oil
   supplements.
EPR Abbreviation for electrophrenic respiration, also called diaphragm pacing, in which electrical stimulation helps
   activate the diaphragm in selected patients with respiratory muscle paralysis.
EPT Abbreviation for estrogen/progestin therapy, treatment using both an estrogen and a progestin, commonly
   discussed in menopausal hormone therapy when the uterus is present.
ER Abbreviation for emergency room or emergency department, the hospital service that evaluates and treats urgent
   illness and injury.
FCC In medicine, an abbreviation for familial colorectal cancer; in other contexts it may have nonmedical meanings.
FFI Abbreviation for fatal familial insomnia, a rare inherited prion disease causing progressively severe insomnia,
    autonomic dysfunction, and neurologic decline.
FISH Abbreviation for fluorescence in situ hybridization, a test that uses fluorescent DNA probes to detect specific
   genes, chromosomes, or chromosomal rearrangements in cells.
FLAP Abbreviation for 5-lipoxygenase-activating protein, a protein encoded by ALOX5AP that helps produce
   leukotrienes involved in inflammation.
GALT Abbreviation for gut-associated lymphoid tissue, immune tissue in the gastrointestinal tract that samples
   intestinal contents and helps defend against pathogens.
GBV-C Abbreviation for GB virus C, also called human pegivirus, a blood-borne virus that can persist in people
   but is not established as a cause of chronic hepatitis.
GD In the RxList medical-dictionary context, abbreviation for Gaucher disease, an inherited lysosomal storage
   disorder caused by deficient glucocerebrosidase.
GI Abbreviation for gastrointestinal, relating to the digestive tract from the mouth through the anus and its
   associated organs.
GPO Abbreviation for group purchasing organization, an organization that combines buyers’ purchasing power to
   negotiate prices and contracts for medicines, supplies, or services.
HAART Abbreviation for highly active antiretroviral therapy, an older term for combination antiretroviral treatment
  used to suppress HIV replication and preserve immune function.
HAPE Abbreviation for high-altitude pulmonary edema, a life-threatening accumulation of fluid in the lungs after
   rapid ascent; immediate descent and supplemental oxygen are urgent treatments.
HAV Abbreviation for hepatitis A virus, an RNA virus spread mainly by the fecal–oral route that causes acute
   hepatitis but usually does not cause chronic infection.
HBV Abbreviation for hepatitis B virus, a DNA virus transmitted through infected blood or body fluids that can
   cause acute or chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis or liver cancer.
HEPA Abbreviation for high-efficiency particulate air, describing a filter designed to remove a very high proportion
   of airborne particles of specified sizes from an air stream.
HGD Commonly an abbreviation for high-grade dysplasia, a marked abnormality of cell development that may be a
  precursor to invasive cancer but is not itself invasive cancer.
HNP Abbreviation for herniated nucleus pulposus, in which the inner material of an intervertebral disk protrudes
  through the outer ring and may compress a nerve root.
HPS Common medical abbreviations include hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, a severe respiratory illness, and
   Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome, an inherited disorder with oculocutaneous albinism and platelet-storage abnor-
   malities; context determines the meaning.

2158
HS Commonly an abbreviation for hereditary spherocytosis, an inherited hemolytic anemia; it can also mean
   half-strength, heart sounds, hamstrings, heparan sulfate, hernia sac, or house surgeon, so context is essential.
HSA Abbreviation that may mean a US health savings account or human serum albumin, the main plasma protein
   that helps maintain oncotic pressure; context determines the meaning.
ICU Abbreviation for intensive care unit, a hospital unit providing continuous monitoring and specialized support
   for critically ill patients.
ID A context-dependent abbreviation that may mean infectious disease, infectious diseases specialist, intellectual
   disability, or identification; the surrounding clinical text determines the meaning.
IFA Abbreviation for indirect fluorescent antibody, a laboratory method that detects antibodies or antigens using
    fluorescent labels, commonly in serologic testing.
IHS Abbreviation for the Indian Health Service, a US federal agency providing health services to American Indians
   and Alaska Native people and communities.
IPT Abbreviation for interpersonal therapy, a structured psychotherapy that focuses on relationships, grief, role
   transitions, and interpersonal difficulties.
IPV Abbreviation for inactivated polio vaccine, an injectable vaccine containing killed poliovirus and used to prevent
   poliomyelitis.
IQ Abbreviation for intelligence quotient, a standardized score from cognitive testing; it describes performance on
    specified tests and is not a complete measure of a person’s abilities or worth.
ITC Abbreviation for in-the-canal, describing a hearing aid or other device positioned within the ear canal.
ITN Abbreviation for insecticide-treated bednet, a net treated with insecticide to reduce mosquito bites and malaria
   transmission.
IVC Commonly abbreviation for inferior vena cava, the large vein returning blood from the lower body to the heart;
   it can also mean intravenous cholangiogram, an X-ray study of the biliary system.
JIP Abbreviation for juvenile intestinal polyposis, an inherited condition in which children develop multiple hamar-
    tomatous polyps in the gastrointestinal tract and may have increased cancer risk.
KB In medical usage, an abbreviation for keratoderma blennorrhagicum or kilobase of DNA; lower-case kb is preferred
   for kilobase, so context is important.
KUB Abbreviation for kidney, ureter, and bladder, commonly referring to a plain abdominal X-ray used to assess
  urinary tract calculi, bowel gas patterns, or other abdominal findings.
L Abbreviation for liter, a metric unit of volume equal to 1,000 milliliters.
LAVH Abbreviation for laparoscopically assisted vaginal hysterectomy, removal of the uterus through the vagina
   with laparoscopic assistance.
LL Commonly an abbreviation for lower lid of the eye or lower limit; the intended meaning depends on the clinical
   context.
LLL Abbreviation for the left lower lobe of the lung.
LLQ Abbreviation for left lower quadrant, usually referring to the lower-left quarter of the abdomen.
LMP Abbreviation for last menstrual period, the first day of the most recent menstrual bleeding, used in estimating
   gestational age when the date is reliable.
LPA LPA abbreviates Little People of America and may also refer to the left pulmonary artery.
LUL Abbreviation for the left upper lobe of the lung.
LUQ Abbreviation for the left upper quadrant of the abdomen.
LVF Abbreviation for left ventricular failure, meaning failure of the left side of the heart; it may also mean left
   ventricular function, depending on context.

                                                                                                                2159
MAOI Abbreviation for monoamine oxidase inhibitor, a drug that inhibits monoamine oxidase and is used in selected
  treatment of depression and other disorders.
MAP Common abbreviation for Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis, an organism of the M. avium
  complex; the abbreviation can have other meanings in different clinical contexts.
MCD An abbreviation with several medical meanings, including minimal change disease, mean corpuscular diameter,
  and medullary cystic disease; the intended meaning depends on context.
MCP Membrane cofactor protein, also called CD46, is a cell-surface protein that regulates complement activation
  and helps protect host cells from complement-mediated injury; the abbreviation can have other meanings in
  different contexts.
MDI An abbreviation that may mean metered-dose inhaler, multiple daily injections, or mental developmental index;
  the intended meaning depends on context.
MEDVAC Abbreviation for medical evacuation: the transport of ill or injured people to a medical facility or to a
  location providing a higher level of care.
MI Abbreviation for myocardial infarction, or heart attack: death of heart-muscle tissue caused by prolonged
   inadequate blood flow, usually from acute coronary artery blockage.
MM An abbreviation that may mean meningomyelocele, malignant melanoma, or multiple myeloma; in lowercase,
  mm commonly means millimeter. The intended meaning depends on context.
MP Abbreviation for mercaptopurine, a purine-antimetabolite drug, or for molecular pathology; the intended meaning
   depends on context.
MPS Abbreviation for mucopolysaccharidosis, a group of inherited lysosomal storage disorders caused by deficient
  breakdown of glycosaminoglycans.
MSG Abbreviation for monosodium glutamate, the sodium salt of glutamic acid used as a flavor enhancer and
   contributing umami taste.
MTX Abbreviation for methotrexate, a folate-antagonist drug used in selected cancers, autoimmune diseases, and
  other conditions.
MVP Abbreviation for mitral valve prolapse, in which one or both mitral-valve leaflets bow into the left atrium
  during ventricular systole; it is often mild but can sometimes cause mitral regurgitation or arrhythmias.
MYH MYH is a gene-family abbreviation involving myosin or DNA-repair proteins; the specific gene and variant
  determine the clinical meaning.
ND ND is a context-dependent abbreviation that may mean naturopathic doctor, neurodevelopmental, or another
   term; the full meaning should be specified.
NEP NEP is a context-dependent abbreviation that may mean neuroendocrine pancreatic tumor, nasoendotracheal
   procedure, or another clinical term.
NF NF is a context-dependent abbreviation, including neurofibromatosis, a group of genetic disorders causing
   nerve-sheath tumors and other features.
NG NG commonly means nasogastric, referring to a tube passed through the nose into the stomach, but the
   abbreviation has other uses.
NS NS is a context-dependent abbreviation, commonly normal saline, a sterile sodium-chloride solution, or not
   significant; the full term should be stated.
OB OB is an abbreviation commonly meaning obstetrics, the care of pregnancy, labor, birth, and the postpartum
   period, but it may have other meanings.
OBS OBS is a context-dependent abbreviation that may mean observation, obstetric service, or organic brain
   syndrome; the intended term should be written out.



2160
OCG OCG is a context-dependent abbreviation that may refer to oral contraceptive guidance, oculocardiac testing,
   or another clinical term; the full term should be specified.
OMS An abbreviation for oral and maxillofacial surgery; the intended meaning depends on the clinical context.
PAP PAP is an abbreviation with context-dependent meanings, including Papanicolaou testing, pulmonary alveolar
   proteinosis, or prostatic acid phosphatase; the full term should be specified.
PAS PAS is an abbreviation that may mean periodic-acid–Schiff staining, para-aminosalicylic acid, or pulmonary-
   artery systolic pressure; context determines the meaning.
PAT PAT is a context-dependent abbreviation that may refer to paroxysmal atrial tachycardia, a rapid rhythm
   beginning in the atria, or another clinical term.
PCA PCA is a context-dependent abbreviation, commonly meaning patient-controlled analgesia, in which a patient
   activates prescribed doses from an infusion device.
PCT PCT is a context-dependent abbreviation that may mean procalcitonin, porphyria cutanea tarda, or patient-care
   technician; the full term should be specified.
PDR PDR commonly means Physicians’ Desk Reference, a drug-information reference, but the abbreviation has
   other uses and should be interpreted in context.
PEP PEP is a context-dependent abbreviation, including post-exposure prophylaxis, a preventive medicine course
   after a possible infection exposure.
PHS PHS is an abbreviation whose meaning depends on context, including public health service or primary
   hyperhidrosis; the full term should be specified.
PI PI is a context-dependent abbreviation, including principal investigator, pulmonary insufficiency, or protease
    inhibitor; the intended meaning must be specified.
PLP PLP commonly means pyridoxal 5′ -phosphate, the active coenzyme form of vitamin B6 required by many
   enzymes, but the abbreviation has other uses.
PMD PMD is a context-dependent abbreviation, including Pelizaeus–Merzbacher disease, a rare inherited disorder
  of central myelination, or a professional medical designation.
PON PON is a context-dependent abbreviation that may refer to postoperative nausea, paraoxonase, or another
   clinical term; the full meaning should be stated.
PTU PTU is the abbreviation for propylthiouracil, an antithyroid medicine used selectively because of liver toxicity
   and other safety considerations.
PV PV is a context-dependent abbreviation, including polycythemia vera, plasma volume, or peripheral vision; the
   full term should be specified.
PVB PVB is a context-dependent abbreviation that may mean paravertebral block, a regional anesthetic technique,
   or another medical term.
PX PX is a context-dependent abbreviation that may mean prognosis, patient, prescription, or a genetic marker;
   clinical documentation should spell out the intended term.
Q.2H A prescription abbreviation meaning “every 2 hours.” Medication instructions should use clear wording because
   abbreviation misinterpretation can cause dosing errors.
Q.3H. A prescription abbreviation meaning “every 3 hours.” Medication instructions should use clear wording because
   abbreviation misinterpretation can cause dosing errors.
Q.S. A prescription abbreviation from the Latin “quantum sufficiat,” meaning “quantity sufficient” to make the
    required amount or concentration. The exact quantity must be specified by the formulation or prescription
    context.
R/O R/O is an abbreviation for rule out, indicating that a condition is being considered but has not been confirmed;
   clear documentation should state the actual diagnostic question.

                                                                                                              2161
RAD Acronym whose medical meaning depends on context, commonly radiation absorbed dose or right axis deviation
   on an ECG.
RBC RBC is the abbreviation for red blood cell, the cell that transports oxygen with hemoglobin and carries carbon
   dioxide back toward the lungs.
RF RF is a context-dependent abbreviation, including rheumatoid factor, radiofrequency, or risk factor; the complete
   term should be stated.
RLL RLL is the abbreviation for right lower lobe, usually referring to the lower lobe of the right lung.
RLQ RLQ is the abbreviation for right lower quadrant of the abdomen, containing structures including the appendix,
   cecum, and right adnexa.
RML RML is the abbreviation for right middle lobe, the middle lobe of the right lung.
RP RP is a context-dependent abbreviation, commonly retinitis pigmentosa, an inherited retinal degeneration causing
   night blindness and progressive visual-field loss.
RUQ RUQ is the abbreviation for right upper quadrant of the abdomen, containing the liver, gallbladder, duodenum,
   and portions of bowel and kidney.
SGOT SGOT is the former abbreviation for AST, an enzyme measured in blood that can rise with injury to liver,
   heart, muscle, or other tissues.
SGPT SGPT is the former abbreviation for ALT, a liver-associated enzyme that rises in many forms of hepatocellular
   injury.
SHP SHP is a context-dependent abbreviation that may refer to a healthcare professional, a gene or protein, or
   another clinical term; the full meaning should be specified.
SLV SLV is a context-dependent abbreviation that may mean single-lung ventilation, serum lithium value, or another
   term; the full meaning should be specified.
STD(S) Abbreviation for sexually transmitted disease(s), now often called sexually transmitted infections.
STS STS is a context-dependent abbreviation that may mean soft-tissue sarcoma, sodium thiosulfate, or another
   clinical term; the full term should be stated.
TMR TMR is a context-dependent abbreviation, including targeted muscle reinnervation, a surgical technique used
  to improve control of a prosthesis and reduce amputation pain.
TPA/TPA Abbreviation for tissue plasminogen activator.
TSD TSD is a context-dependent abbreviation that may mean total sleep deprivation, traumatic stress disorder, or
   another clinical term; the full term should be specified.
TSE TSE is a context-dependent abbreviation, including transmissible spongiform encephalopathy, the prion-disease
   group that includes Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
UL UL is a context-dependent abbreviation that may mean upper limit, ulnar or ulna-related, or another clinical
   term; the full meaning should be specified.
URG URG is a context-dependent abbreviation that may refer to urinary urgency or an urgent clinical priority;
   documentation should state the full term.
URTI Abbreviation for upper respiratory tract infection, commonly involving the nose, sinuses, pharynx, or larynx
   and often caused by viruses.
VD Abbreviation for venereal disease, an older term for a sexually transmitted infection.
WBS Abbreviation for Williams–Beuren syndrome, a genetic condition associated with characteristic facial features,
  developmental differences, and cardiovascular disease. In other clinical contexts, WBS may have a different
  meaning, so the full term should be specified.

                                 Common Diseases

Scope: This reference-oriented list organizes common human diseases by organ system and clinical domain. It is
a curated, high-importance list rather than a prevalence ranking, and some diseases appear under more than one
heading where they are clinically relevant to several systems. It is not an exhaustive index of every term in the
dictionary. Entries named as syndromes are covered in the companion appendix, Common Syndromes; conditions
conventionally classified as disorders are covered in Common Disorders; and clinical findings, lesions, congenital
anomalies, and injuries are covered in their own companion appendices. Individual symptoms, signs, and laboratory
findings are defined as dictionary entries rather than listed here.

Clinical Note: For a comprehensive medical dictionary, it is essential to distinguish symptoms (subjective experiences
reported by the patient, such as nausea or pain) from clinical signs (objectively observed physical findings detected
on examination, such as jaundice, edema, or tachycardia). Mixing them is common in general health lists, but an
authoritative reference maintains clear separation among Symptoms, Clinical Signs, Syndromes, and Diseases/Disorders
categories.

2196
 Conditions That May Be Asymptomatic

Scope: This reference list groups diseases, infections, and other conditions that may be present without noticeable
symptoms, particularly during early, latent, or compensated stages. Being asymptomatic is a clinical state or mode
of presentation rather than a separate category of disease, so every condition here also belongs under its usual
organ-system or specialty heading, and “May be asymptomatic” is best treated as an attribute or tag in addition to
that classification. Many of these conditions cause symptoms in some people and none in others, and some come to
attention only through screening or when a complication appears. The list is a curated, high-importance reference
rather than a prevalence ranking, and some conditions appear under more than one heading where they are clinically
relevant to several systems. Individual symptoms, signs, and laboratory findings are defined as dictionary entries
rather than listed here.
Important distinction: “Asymptomatic disease” is not a distinct disease; it describes how a disease presents.
Hypertension is a cardiovascular disease that is often asymptomatic, chlamydia is an infection that is frequently
asymptomatic, osteoporosis is a skeletal disease that is typically asymptomatic until a fracture, and open-angle
glaucoma is an eye disease that is often asymptomatic in its early stages.

Cardiovascular Hypertension; Atherosclerosis; Coronary Artery Disease; Peripheral Artery Disease; Some Arrhyth-
    mias; Early Valvular Heart Disease
Metabolic & Endocrine Prediabetes; Early Type 2 Diabetes; Dyslipidemia; Subclinical Hypothyroidism; Subclini-
   cal Hyperthyroidism; Hyperuricemia
Kidney & Urinary Early Chronic Kidney Disease; Diabetic Kidney Disease; Mild Proteinuria; Microscopic Hema-
    turia; Some Kidney Stones
Liver Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD); Chronic Hepatitis B; Chronic Hepatitis
    C; Early Cirrhosis; Hemochromatosis
Infectious HIV Infection During Clinical Latency; Hepatitis B; Hepatitis C; Chlamydia; Gonorrhea; HPV Infection;
    Latent Tuberculosis Infection; Some COVID-19 Infections

   Early Kidney Cancer; Some Thyroid Cancers; Early Breast Cancer
